realLife: Random forests are a dependable default for tabular data because they need little tuning.
summary: Average many different trees and the noise cancels out.
headline: Many noisy trees make one steady vote
overview: Each tree sees a random resample of the data and, at each split, only a random subset of the features. They disagree in different ways, so their average is steadier than any one tree.
More trees help, but only up to a point. After that the picture stops changing.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Use a single deep tree. The boundary is jagged and unstable. Raise the number of trees and watch it smooth out.

check.question: Why does averaging many trees help?
options: Their different errors partly cancel, lowering variance

data: Same shapes as before. Each tree is trained on a bootstrap resample with one randomly chosen feature available at each split, and the forest averages their probabilities.
maths: Variance of an average of B trees falls when the trees are not perfectly correlated.
Breiman's original forest takes a majority vote. scikit-learn averages predicted probabilities instead.
code:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
m = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_features='sqrt').fit(X, y)

sources.title: scikit-learn: ensemble methods
sources.note: bootstrap samples, feature subsets, averaging probabilities, variance reduction at slight bias cost
